questions.title: How can I keep a React list responsive with thousands of rows?
questions.content: I am building an activity view that can contain several thousand rows. Rendering the full list makes scrolling feel sluggish. What approaches work well for keeping the interface responsive while preserving keyboard navigation and screen-reader support?

questions.title: What is a safe way to retry failed fetch requests?
questions.content: Our client occasionally gets transient network errors when requesting a JSON API. I want to retry safely without duplicating writes or overwhelming the service. How should I structure retries, timeouts, and backoff for read requests?

questions.title: How do I share typed metadata between Next.js layouts and pages?
questions.content: I have route metadata and page data that both need a small set of typed values. I would like to avoid repeating the same query while keeping the page output predictable. Which Next.js patterns are a good fit?

answers.content:
For large collections, windowing is usually the biggest win: render only the visible range plus a small overscan. Libraries such as TanStack Virtual handle measurement and scrolling, while your row components still need stable keys and semantic structure. Keep focus behavior explicit when rows mount and unmount, and test with keyboard and assistive technology. If the data can be grouped or paged, that can further reduce the amount of work.

I would first profile the list, then add virtualization only where it improves the real bottleneck.

Also check whether each row causes broad state updates. Memoizing expensive row work can help, but virtualization generally matters more once the DOM itself becomes large. Make sure the list has an accessible label and that the virtualized container exposes an appropriate scroll region.

Use retries only for requests that are safe to repeat, such as GET requests, and cap the number of attempts. An exponential delay with jitter helps avoid synchronized retry spikes. Set a request timeout, honor server retry guidance when available, and do not retry validation or authorization failures. For mutations, use an idempotency key or avoid automatic retries unless the endpoint guarantees idempotence.

answerTemplates: Start by measuring the current behavior, then choose the smallest change that addresses the bottleneck. Keep the contract explicit and add a focused test for the edge case.
A practical approach is to separate input validation from the operation itself. Return a consistent error shape and make retries safe only when the operation is idempotent.
Prefer the built-in framework mechanism where possible, and verify the behavior at the boundary where data enters the system. This keeps the implementation easier to maintain.
The tradeoff depends on data size and update frequency. Begin with a simple implementation, collect metrics, and add caching or concurrency only when the evidence points there.
Make the state transition explicit and test both the success and failure paths. In particular, check keyboard behavior, loading states, and what happens when the network is unavailable.
